newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Organisers try to play down Dalai Lama Taiwan trip.
newsitem.headline: Organisers try to play down Dalai Lama Taiwan trip.

text.p: Taiwan and Tibetan organisers on Friday made a last effort to play down the political nature of the Dalai Lama's visit, saying the Tibetan spiritual leader had come for a religious visit.

"The Dalai Lama was jointly invited by 10 Taiwan religious groups, and his trip is purely religious. We regret that his scheduled visit is politicised," Buddhist Master Ching Hsin, one of the Dalai Lama's Taiwan hosts, told reporters.
The Dalai Lama's visit has angered the communist government in Beijing, which steadfastly claims that both Taiwan and Tibet are inalienable parts of China.
Ching said politicisation of the Tibetan exiled leader's visit, scheduled on March 22-27, has hurt the Tibetan god-king.
Local media have repeatedly reported that Ching would accompany the Dalai Lama to meet Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on either March 26 or March 27.
Lee has expressed his desire to meet the Dalai Lama, saying he would not miss the chance of such a meeting since he was an important leader.
No such meeting has been announced by Lee's office.
Beijing has lashed out at the Dalai Lama's journey and specifically at his expected meeting with Lee, branding both men as "splittists" bent on independence from China.
Gyalor Thondup, the second brother of the Dalai Lama, acknowledged that the exiled leader's trip was important.
"It is extremely important for the Dalai Lama to visit Taiwan. It is an historic event," said Thondup who arrived in Taipei on March 18 as the Dalai Lama's advance party.
"For the past 30-odd years, your people have continued to ask the Dalai Lama to visit Taiwan, and the long-awaited trip has finally materialised," he said.
Ching Hsin said the Taiwan organisers would leave March 27 open for the Dalai Lama's own arrangements, and the Tibetan exiled leader is expected to leave Taiwan at noon on that day.

Karma Gelek Yuthok, representative of the Dalai Lama's liaison office in Japan, who arranged his Taiwan visit, said the Tibetan exiled leader would not visit Taiwan's parliament because of the visit's "religious and cultural" nature.

Taiwan's parliament has invited the Dalai Lama to speak, and pro-independence deputies have demanded that the government welcome the Tibetan spiritual leader as a state guest instead of a religious leader.

Yuthok brushed aside allegations that the Dalai Lama would charge for his visit. Local newspapers had said the Tibetan god-king would be able to earn more than T$20 million (US$727,000) giving Buddhist lectures in Taiwan.
"It is not in accordance with the Buddhist tradition to charge fees or demand payments for religious teachings," Yuthok said.

"However, it is customary and permissible to make donations for such teachings. The organisers ... have sought contributions in the form of voluntary donations, and not in the form of fees or commercial payments," he said.
